parts: Lesson 19: My Family and I — Summary

A family is a fundamental unit of society whose members are related by marriage, blood or adoption and share a common roof, kitchen and source of income. A nuclear family is a couple and their children (natural or adopted) living together; a joint family has parents and siblings of the couple (three generations) living together. A family provides protection from danger to life, emotional bonding, financial and emotional security, preparation for life through education, passing of socio-cultural values, and recreation.

Beginning stage: independent young adult and marriage. Expanding stage: starts with the birth of the first child; parenting – the most challenging stage. Contracting stage: starts when the first child leaves home and ends with the last child leaving or the passing away of either partner; couples retire, pursue hobbies, take part in community service and enjoy grandchildren. Understanding the cycle helps to foresee challenges and plan priorities. Beginning stage needs: commitment, compatibility, trust, attachment; marriage should not be before 18 for a girl and 21 for a boy; preparation includes counselling on adjustment, tolerance, patience, coping with stress, financial re-planning and health security. Guidelines for healthy relationships: talk courteously, listen, be conscious of facial expressions, help each other, share responsibilities equally, look after the sick, share plans with family and express appreciation; avoid rude talk, body gestures and negative facial expressions, criticism and going out without informing. To help a new bride adjust: welcome her, accept her as part of the family, give her time and space, be realistic and non-critical.

Pregnancy: nutritious food at frequent intervals, rest and exercise, a happy atmosphere and regular check-ups; the husband and family should share work. Infancy: feeding (exclusive breast milk for 6 months), loving, clothing, bathing, immunisation; working parents may use grandparents, neighbours, day care or crèche (near home or workplace, clean, open, ventilated, qualified staff, on-call doctor, flexible timings) or a verified helper. Young children: growth depends on heredity (cannot be changed – colour of eyes, skin, height, build) and environment (managed by the parents): early stimulation, play and discipline. Infants up to two years play solitary games; children of 3–5 years play make-believe games; older children play board, computer and outdoor games that teach cooperation, sharing, team spirit and leadership; toys should be safe, inexpensive, durable, interesting and attractive, and may be low-cost and home-made.

Discipline styles: autocratic – restrictions and punishment; children lack self-confidence, are anxious, have poor communication and may become rebellious. Democratic – children are independent but under parental control, can express opinions, parents are warm and open; children are socially well adjusted, responsible and self-confident. Permissive – parents are totally uninvolved; children develop no self-control, lack social skills. School-going children (7–8 years) need little help in eating and bathing, support in studies, a separate study space, group games and good eating habits. Adolescents seek independence and identity; parents should set rules and limits, be firm yet flexible, keep communication open, trust them and give emotional support. Preparation for a career should begin early. The elderly should accept ageing, slow down and let others help; families should help them in tasks, spend time with them, meet nutritional and medical needs, involve them in decisions and respect their views.

Good family relations need understanding of duties, empathy, sensitivity, effective verbal and non-verbal communication, concern and love, help, and discretion; these are life skills. Mistrust, criticism, interference, self-centredness, lack of empathy and poor communication cause disharmony. Values (respect for elders, honesty, truthfulness, humility) are learnt in the family by direct teaching and by the parents' own example. Girls and women should not be discriminated against in nutrition, education, play, jobs or expressing opinions; equality is shown by equal nutrition, education and opportunities, recognising their contribution and respect.
